Grade 3 · Unit 3.1

Forces, Motion, and Magnets

Why do objects speed up, slow down, turn, or stay still?

Forces explain why things speed up, slow down, turn or stay put. You will compare balanced and unbalanced forces, use patterns in motion to predict what happens next, explore magnets and static electricity that push and pull without touching, and design a way to move something using magnets.

In this lesson

  1. Balanced and unbalanced forces
  2. Motion patterns help predict
  3. Forces without touching
  4. Magnet design problem
  5. Try it at home
  6. Check yourself

Concept 1

Balanced and unbalanced forces

Balanced forces keep motion the same; unbalanced forces change motion.

Try it

Fair-test and CER refresher

two toy cars on the same ramp and sentence cards labeled Claim, Evidence, Reasoning.

“Change one thing at a time, like the ramp height. If we change the car and the ramp together, we do not know which one changed the distance.”

“Claim: What we think. Evidence: What we measured. Reasoning: Why it fits.”

You did this before / what is new: You used fair tests and CER cards in Unit 0; now you use them to investigate forces.

Analogy

Tug-of-war

equal teams vs unequal teams.

“Equal pulls balance. Unequal pulls move the rope.”

Try it

Push the car

toy car on table.

“Push gently. Push harder. Watch the motion change.”

“Now flick a marble across a very smooth tray and mark its position every second. When friction is small, the gaps between marks stay almost the same: the forces on it are nearly balanced, so its motion hardly changes. On rough carpet the gaps shrink quickly, because friction is a force against the motion and nothing balances it.”

You did this before / what is new: You pushed and pulled objects in K-A; now you collect evidence about balanced and unbalanced forces.

Diagram

Force arrows

box with equal arrows and unequal arrows.

“Same arrows: no change. Different arrows: motion changes.”

Concept 2

Motion patterns help predict

If motion repeats, we can predict what happens next.

Try it

Rolling ball track

ball rolling down a ramp and across floor.

“Mark where the ball stops. Repeat. Find the pattern.”

You did this before / what is new: You moved objects in K-A; now you use repeated motion to make a prediction.

Data

Dot diagram

ball positions each second.

“Close dots mean slow. Far dots mean fast.”

Concept 3

Forces without touching

Magnets and static electricity can push or pull without direct touch.

Try it

Magnet explorer

magnet near paper clip, penny, foil, eraser.

“Test many objects. Which ones stick? Write yes or no for each one.”

Try it

Static demo

rubbed balloon near paper bits or a thin stream of water.

“Rub the balloon. Hold it near paper bits. The paper jumps. Ask: What happens when the balloon is farther away?”

Diagram

Magnet field

magnet with curved field lines.

“The force is strongest near the ends. It can pass through thin paper.”

Real world

Compass

compass needle.

“Earth acts like a giant magnet. The compass points north.”

Magnet design problem

Hands-on · Design or investigate

Try it at home or in class

Design a paper-clip mover that moves a paper clip at least 20 cm without touching the clip directly. Criteria: the clip moves the full distance. Constraints: one magnet, one paper clip, paper or card, and no direct touching. Students test, record evidence, and improve the design.

Try it

What you need

toy car, cardboard ramp, books, tape, small ball, index cards, pencil, paper, 2 ring or bar magnets, paper clips, balloon, small paper bits, string.

Safety: keep magnets away from Chromebooks and other electronics. Use only large ceramic or ferrite magnets; small, very strong magnets can be swallowed and are dangerous. Keep every magnet out of mouths. Do the water-stream static demo over a tray, keep water away from Chromebooks, and dry hands before touching a keyboard.

Try it

What you do

test gentle vs harder pushes; roll a ball and mark positions; make a dot diagram; test magnets on objects; do the balloon static demo; design a paper-clip mover that moves without direct touch.

No time or no good weather? Use this data

This data is a backup. It lets you practice reading evidence, but the standard expects you to collect your own when you can.

students record ball or car positions and magnet tests.

dot-position table for a model ball with no friction (a real ball on a floor slows down, so its dots get closer together; students should notice this in their own data): 0 cm, 10 cm, 20 cm, 30 cm at 0, 1, 2, 3 seconds; students predict 40 cm. A second backup set, also a model ball with no friction: 0 cm, 8 cm, 16 cm, 24 cm; predict 32 cm. Both sets are models: even gaps mean balanced forces. A real ball on carpet has friction, so its gaps shrink, for example 0, 9, 16, 21 cm (gaps 9, 7, 5). Do not predict 40 cm for a real ball; predict a smaller gap each second.

Words to know

force
a push or pull.
balanced forces
forces that cancel, so motion does not change.
unbalanced forces
forces that cause a change in motion.
motion
change in position.
pattern
something that repeats.
magnet
object that attracts some metals.
attract
pull toward.
repel
push away.
static electricity
a charge that can make small objects move without touch.
criterion
what success looks like.
Tutor notes: misconceptions, standards, pacing

Pacing: six 30-minute sessions.

Common misconceptions to listen for:

  • “A force is needed to keep an object moving.” Correct: unbalanced forces change motion; balanced forces do not change motion.
  • “Magnets attract all metals.” Correct: magnets attract things made of iron and some steels; most other metals, like aluminum foil and copper, do not stick.
  • “Forces only work when objects touch.” Correct: magnetic and static-electric forces can act without touching.
  • “A bigger push always makes an object go forever.” Correct: forces can change motion, but friction and other forces can slow objects.

Limits and cautions:

  • Gravity is not taught here; it moves to 5.2.
  • Simple machines are not a grade 3 PE in this unit. They appear only as an application note if the teacher chooses: “A ramp spreads a lift over a longer path.”
  • Static-electricity demos can fail on humid days; the provided question prompts and magnet investigation still earn 3-PS2-3.
  • Friction is simplified as a force that can slow motion. Deeper force models come in later grades.

Michigan Science Standards this unit earns:

  • 3-PS2-1: Plan and carry out an investigation to determine the effect of balanced and unbalanced forces on motion.
  • 3-PS2-2: Make observations or measurements of an object’s motion to show that a pattern can predict future motion.
  • 3-PS2-3: Ask questions about electric or magnetic interactions between objects that are not touching.
  • 3-PS2-4: Define a simple design problem that can be solved using magnet ideas.
  • 3-5-ETS1-1: Define a simple design problem with criteria and constraints.
  • 3-5-ETS1-2: Generate and compare possible solutions.
  • 3-5-ETS1-3: Plan and carry out fair tests.

Connections: Builds on: K-A Pushes and Pulls; Unit 0: How Science Works. Builds toward: 4.1 Energy, Speed, and Collisions; 5.2 Gravity, Stars, and Sky Patterns; Unit 3 Forces, Motion & Energy; Unit 8.1 Contact Forces & Collisions; Unit 8.3 Forces at a Distance.
